chunks: From him, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Ubaydah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man from us who buys from the ruler the camels and sheep of the charity (zakat), while he knows that they take from the people more than the obligatory due. He said, so he said: 'The camels and sheep are no different from wheat, barley, and other such goods; there is no harm in buying them until he recognizes the forbidden portion with his own eyes.'

It was said to him: 'And what do you think of the charity collector who comes to us, takes the charity of our sheep, and we say to him, 'Sell them,' so he sells them to us; what do you think about buying them from him?' He said: 'If he has taken them and separated them, there is no harm.'

It was said to him: 'And what do you think about wheat and barley, when the distributor comes to us, distributes our share and takes his share, and separates it with a measure; what do you think about buying that food from him?' He said: 'If he has taken it with a measure while you are present at that, there is no harm in buying it without a measure.'
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to buy zakat animals or grain from the government if they take more than the required amount?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) clarifies that zakat livestock and grains are treated like general commodities, permitting their purchase from collectors even if they have over-collected, provided the specific forbidden portion is not distinctly identified by the buyer. This ruling emphasizes the principle of *istishab* (presumption of permissibility) in commercial transactions, distinguishing between the intrinsic impurity of the excess and the physical separation of goods, thereby facilitating market circulation of zakat assets.
